items.title: 6.1.2 General Form of an Equation of a Circle

source_refs.note: Book p. 165-166: Theorem 2 (general form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0) with proof by completing the square; Note (i) point circle, (ii) imaginary circle

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
If we open the brackets of the standard form \((x - h)^{2} + (y - k)^{2} = r^{2}\) we get
\[x^{2} + y^{2} - 2hx - 2ky + (h^{2} + k^{2} - r^{2}) = 0\]
Every circle therefore has an equation with: \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) with equal coefficients, no \(xy\) term, and some \(x\), \(y\) and constant terms. Writing the coefficients as \(2g\), \(2f\) and \(c\) gives the general form below; the 2s are chosen so that halving is easy later.
Theorem 2: The equation \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\) ...(1) where \(g, f, c \in \mathbb{R}\) represents a circle.

Proof: Equation (1) can be written as: \(x^{2} + 2gx + y^{2} + 2fy = -c\)
Completing the square for \(x\) and \(y\), we add \(g^{2} + f^{2}\) to both sides:
\[(x^{2} + 2gx + g^{2})\]
\[+ (y^{2} + 2fy + f^{2})\]
\[= g^{2} + f^{2} - c\]
This gives
\[(x + g)^{2} + (y + f)^{2} = \left(\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\right)^{2}\]
Alternatively, this can be written as
\[[x - (-g)]^{2} + [y - (-f)]^{2}\]
\[= \left(\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\right)^{2}\]
which is the general form of the equation of a circle with centre \((-g, -f)\) and radius \(r = \sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\), provided \(g^{2} + f^{2} - c > 0\).
Hence equation (1) represents a circle under the condition \(g^{2} + f^{2} - c > 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why add \(g^{2}\)? To make \(x^{2} + 2gx\) a perfect square we add the square of half the coefficient of \(x\): half of \(2g\) is \(g\), so we add \(g^{2}\) and get \((x + g)^{2}\). The same for \(y\): add \(f^{2}\). Whatever is added on the left must be added on the right.
So: centre \((-g, -f)\) is minus half the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\); the radius is \(\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\).
An equation of the second degree \(ax^{2} + by^{2} + 2hxy + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\) can represent a circle only if \(a = b \ne 0\) and \(h = 0\) (equal coefficients of \(x^{2}\), \(y^{2}\) and no \(xy\) term). If \(a = b \ne 1\), first divide by \(a\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
(i) If \(g^{2} + f^{2} - c = 0\), equation (1) represents a point circle with centre \((-g, -f)\).
(ii) If \(g^{2} + f^{2} - c < 0\), equation (1) represents no real locus (an imaginary circle).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. General form: \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\).
2. Centre \((-g, -f)\), radius \(\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\).
3. \(g^{2} + f^{2} - c > 0\): real circle; \(= 0\): point circle; \(< 0\): imaginary circle (no real locus).
4. A second-degree equation is a circle only if the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are equal and there is no \(xy\) term.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking the centre as \((g, f)\) or as (coefficient of \(x\), coefficient of \(y\)); it is \((-g, -f)\), half the coefficients with signs changed.
2. Using the general-form rule before making the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) equal to 1.
3. Writing the radius as \(\sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} + c}\): the constant is subtracted.
